name: Macro tracking / IIFYM

lead: Macro tracking means hitting daily targets for protein, carbohydrate and fat. IIFYM, 'If It Fits Your Macros', is the flexible version in which any food counts if the numbers fit. Lifters use it to cut fat or build muscle toward a defined physique.

Hitting protein and calorie targets supports fat loss with muscle retention, or muscle gain in a surplus. Protein and calorie targets are well studied; no clinical studies of IIFYM as a named approach were found.

paras: Users log foods in an app against gram targets, and total energy follows from standard factors per macronutrient. Ratios vary with individual goals, and experts disagree on ideal protein amounts.
Few direct risks are documented for the method itself. Logging accuracy depends on label estimates, and as with calorie counting, tracking can be a concern for people with eating-disorder histories.

angle.text: Lifters track macros, often under the flexible IIFYM approach, to drive cutting or bulking toward a leaner, more muscular physique. Protein and calorie targets are well studied; research on macro tracking as a method is limited.

lead: Macro tracking is the practice of logging daily grams of protein, carbohydrate and fat, rather than only total calories. "If It Fits Your Macros" (IIFYM), also called flexible dieting, is the version in which any food is acceptable provided the gram targets are met. People use it to lose body fat while keeping muscle, or to gain muscle with controlled fat gain, which shapes the leaner face, visible muscle definition and fuller physique looksmaxxing communities aim for [1][2].

Energy comes from roughly 4 kcal per gram of protein or carbohydrate and 9 kcal per gram of fat, so macro targets set both calories and the split [2]. Bodybuilding reference material describes the three macronutrients as having ratios that vary with an individual's goals, and notes that experts disagree on ideal protein amounts [1].

IIFYM is widely used among strength athletes: in a 2023 survey of 305 competitive powerlifters, IIFYM/flexible dieting was the most common long-term diet, followed by 78.3 percent of those who reported following one [3]. Research on IIFYM as a named approach to appearance outcomes is limited.
infobox: 4 kcal/g protein and carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g fat [2]

paras: Users set gram targets for each macronutrient, typically with higher protein, and log food in an app. Energy is derived from roughly 4 kcal per gram of protein or carbohydrate and 9 kcal per gram of fat [2]. Bodybuilding literature notes protein recommendations ranging from about 25 to 30 percent of calories, with expert disagreement on the amount [1].

The flexible element is that food choice is not restricted: processed and whole foods both count if targets are hit. Some people mix the approach with more traditional food choices at different phases; on T Nation, one member asked a competitor why he used bodybuilding staples in the off-season but IIFYM foods in contest prep [4].

Practitioners usually start from a calorie target for their goal, then divide it into protein, carbohydrate and fat in grams and log food in an app until each number is hit.[2] The method turns a diet into three daily numbers rather than a list of allowed foods, which is the core of the flexible-dieting idea: any food counts if it fits the targets.

Protein is usually the first target set. Wikipedia's article on protein reports a baseline recommendation of 0.8 g per kg of body weight for sedentary adults, 1.4 to 1.8 g per kg for people doing strength training and aiming at muscle gain, and possibly 1.8 to 2.0 g per kg for athletes dieting to lose weight, in order to help preserve lean muscle.[5] Carbohydrate and fat targets then fill the remaining calories according to preference and training demands.[1]

The appearance logic in physique communities runs in two directions. In a calorie deficit, high protein targets are used to lose fat, which reveals jaw, cheek and abdominal definition, while keeping as much muscle as possible. In a surplus, tracked targets are used to add muscle with a controlled amount of fat so that the physique looks fuller without a large rise in body fat.[1][2]

Competitors in bodybuilding use tracked intake across prep phases. In the 2018 comparison of 41 bodybuilders, males reported an average of about 2,577 kcal, 163 g protein, 323 g carbohydrate and 84 g fat per day.[6]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: Communities discuss macro targets as a refinement of calorie counting for cutting and bulking, particularly to retain muscle while losing facial fat. T Nation members discuss tracking apps and coaching algorithms, and some lifters say they track macros while others prefer not to count at all [7][8]. One member described muscle groups looking flat during a calorie deficit as part of getting leaner [9].

A 2018 comparison of 41 competitive bodybuilders found no significant differences in mean nutrient intakes between those who used macronutrient-based dieting and those who dieted strictly, among males [6].

Older studies of dieting style examine flexible versus rigid restraint, a broader idea than IIFYM. A 1999 study of 223 adults associated flexible dieting with less overeating, lower body mass and lower depression and anxiety, while calorie counting and conscious dieting were associated with overeating when alone [10]. A 2002 study of 188 non-obese women found rigid dieting associated with eating-disorder symptoms and mood disturbance, while flexible dieting was not strongly associated with them [11]. These studies did not test IIFYM macro tracking specifically.
The 2023 survey of 305 competitive powerlifters also records which strategies lifters follow across competitive phases, with flexible dieting among the most reported long-term approaches.[3]

No controlled trials of IIFYM as a named approach to appearance outcomes were found. Related observational and survey research on powerlifters, bodybuilders and flexible versus rigid dieting is summarised above [3][6][10][11].

The flexible-versus-rigid dieting literature is often cited in discussion of tracking. The 2002 study in 188 non-obese women associated rigid control with more eating-disorder symptoms, while flexible control was not strongly associated with them.[11] The 1999 study of 223 adults associated calorie counting with overeating when alone.[10] Neither study measured macro tracking as practised in fitness communities, and researchers do not report macro tracking itself as harmful.
